Linkage: The Exception to Independent Assortment
Mendel and the Foundations of Genetics

blocks.x: Gregor Johann Mendel, an Augustinian friar, is regarded as the "Father of Genetics." He was born in 1822 and carried out his famous hybridization experiments on the garden pea, Pisum sativum, at a monastery in Brünn (Brno). Mendel's experimental design relied on choosing seven traits located on different, non-homologous chromosomes (in modern terms, unlinked genes) — a stroke of good fortune, since it meant none of his traits showed linkage, which would have complicated his ratios. Traits he studied included seed shape (round/wrinkled), seed color (yellow/green), pod shape, pod color, flower color, flower/pod position along the stem, and stem height; notably, location of the pod was not one of the seven characters he selected (he did study flower position, but not "location of pod" as a separate character in the classic list).

Mendel presented his findings in a paper titled "Experiments on Plant Hybridization" ("Versuche über Pflanzenhybriden"), first published in 1866. The work was largely ignored for over three decades until it was rediscovered and republished/reconfirmed in 1900 independently by three botanists — Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak — and Mendel's original paper itself was specifically republished in 1901. Mendel died on 6 January 1884 of chronic nephritis (note: some flawed quiz items misstate the year as 1984 — the correct historical year is 1884). The first Mendelian trait documented in humans is credited to Farabee (1905), who described the inheritance of brachydactyly (short fingers) as a dominant trait in a human pedigree.

Mendel did not propose blending inheritance, linkage, or crossing over — concepts that came later (linkage and crossing over were established by Thomas Hunt Morgan's school working with Drosophila). Mendel is specifically not associated with incomplete dominance, a phenomenon discovered afterward (e.g., by Correns) that his complete-dominance-based pea traits did not display. Mendel also could not have detected linkage in his own data specifically because his chosen genes assorted independently — his traits behaved as if unlinked, so independent assortment (not segregation, dominance, or crossing over) is the reason he never observed linked inheritance.

items: Law of Segregation: The two alleles of a gene carried by a diploid individual separate (segregate) from each other during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele of each gene. This law directly predicts the classic 3:1 phenotypic ratio (and 1:2:1 genotypic ratio) obtained when self-fertilizing an F1 heterozygote. The F2 monohybrid ratio of 1:2:1 (genotypic) is the direct consequence of segregation.

Law of Independent Assortment: Alleles of different genes (on different chromosome pairs) segregate independently of one another during gamete formation. This law is exemplified by the classic dihybrid F2 ratio of 9:3:3:1.

blocks.x: (Mendel's "Law of Dominance" — that one allele can mask the expression of another in a heterozygote — is often listed as a third principle underlying his ratios, though it is sometimes treated as a corollary observation rather than a distinct "law.")
Monohybrid Cross

A cross tracking a single gene with two alleles. Self-fertilizing (selfing) a heterozygote (Aa × Aa) yields F2 offspring in a 3:1 phenotypic ratio (3 dominant-phenotype : 1 recessive-phenotype) and a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio (1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa). For a cross of two heterozygotes such as Tt × Tt, the expected offspring genotypes are 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so the chance of a fully homozygous individual of either type in that single cross is 1/4 TT + 1/4 tt = 50% total, but the chance of the specific homozygous dominant class (TT) alone is 25% (and homozygous recessive tt is also 25% alone) — always check exactly which class a question asks about.
Dihybrid Cross

Tracks two genes simultaneously. Selfing a double heterozygote (AaBb × AaBb), assuming independent assortment, yields the classic F2 phenotypic ratio of 9:3:3:1 (9 both-dominant : 3 dominant/recessive : 3 recessive/dominant : 1 both-recessive). The full F2 genotypic ratio for a dihybrid cross (expanding the 1:2:1 pattern independently across both genes) is 1:2:2:4:2:4:1:2:1 (nine distinct genotypic classes in the proportions 1,2,1,2,4,2,1,2,1). When epistatic gene interactions modify the standard dihybrid ratio, other patterns emerge (see Epistasis below), including ratios such as 3:3:1:1 or similar modified proportions depending on the interaction — a 3:3:1 pattern specifically arises from certain gene-interaction (modified dihybrid) crosses rather than a plain unmodified dihybrid.
Trihybrid Cross

Tracks three independently assorting genes. A trihybrid individual (AaBbCc) heterozygous at all three loci produces 23 = 8 genetically distinct gamete types. Selfing two trihybrids gives the full trihybrid F2 phenotypic ratio of 27:9:9:9:3:3:3:1 (8 classes total, summing to 64 = 43).
Test Cross and Back Cross

items: A test cross crosses an individual of unknown or uncertain genotype (showing the dominant phenotype) with a homozygous recessive individual, to reveal whether the tested individual is homozygous dominant or heterozygous, based on the ratio of offspring phenotypes. It is specifically used to confirm homozygosity or heterozygosity of a genotype. For a dihybrid, a test cross of a double heterozygote (AaBb × aabb) that shows independent assortment produces offspring in a 1:1:1:1 ratio of the four possible phenotypic classes; a 1:1:1:1 test-cross ratio thus indicates the two genes are not linked. A dihybrid cross (not test cross) between two double heterozygotes is the classic way to confirm the law of independent assortment in the first place, by observing the 9:3:3:1 ratio.

A back cross is more general: any cross of an F1 hybrid back to either of its parental lines (which may be homozygous dominant or homozygous recessive). A test cross is technically a special case of a back cross (specifically, a back cross to the homozygous recessive parent).

A cross between an F1 individual and its homozygous recessive parent line specifically is termed a test cross in most contexts (and sometimes also loosely termed a backcross, depending on textbook terminology).

blocks.x: Worked Example: Independent Genes

Classic hog-genetics style problem: gene B (belted, dominant) and gene S (syndactyly, dominant) are on different chromosomes. A cross Bb Ss × bb ss is a double test cross and yields all four phenotypic classes — belted-syndactylous, belted-normal, unbelted-syndactylous, unbelted-normal — each in 25% (1:1:1:1), confirming both genes assort independently and neither shows linkage.

Another representative problem: crossing YY RR (yellow, wrinkled) × yy rr (green, smooth) peas and selfing the F1 (YyRr × YyRr) gives an F2 in the standard 9:3:3:1 ratio. Among the 9/16 that are yellow and wrinkled (dominant for both traits), only the fully homozygous dominant class YYRR is "pure-breeding" (will breed true) — this represents 1/9 of the yellow-wrinkled subgroup (i.e., 1/16 of the total F2, which is 1/9 of the 9/16 yellow-wrinkled fraction).

items: Codominance: Both alleles are simultaneously and fully expressed in the heterozygote, with neither masking the other — the heterozygote shows a distinct phenotype combining both, rather than blending them. Classic example: the mouse esterase electrophoresis case, where a pure fast-form line crossed with a pure slow-form line gives F1 individuals showing both bands simultaneously (not a blend), and F2 in a 1/4 fast : 1/4 slow : 1/2 both ratio — a textbook illustration of codominance. The ABO blood group system in humans is a classic example combining codominance (IA and IB alleles are codominant with each other, giving type AB) with a recessive i allele (see the dedicated blood-groups topic for full detail on antigens, genotypes, and transfusion compatibility). The H antigen precursor needed for ABO antigen expression is produced by the action of a dominant allele (H), not a recessive one.

Incomplete dominance: The heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype that blends features of both homozygotes (e.g., red × white snapdragons giving pink F1), rather than either allele being fully expressed.

Multiple alleles: A single gene locus can have more than two allelic forms circulating in a population, even though any individual carries only two. ABO blood type (alleles IA, IB, i) is the textbook human example of multiple allelism.

blocks.x: Epistasis occurs when the alleles of one gene mask or modify the phenotypic expression of alleles at a different, non-allelic gene locus — a form of gene interaction that alters the expected 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio into other characteristic patterns. Common recognized categories include:

items: Recessive epistasis (9:3:4): A homozygous recessive genotype at one locus masks the phenotype of the second locus.
Dominant epistasis (12:3:1): A dominant allele at one locus masks expression at the second locus.

Duplicate recessive epistasis / complementary gene action (9:7): Two genes must each have at least one dominant allele for the phenotype to appear; if either locus is homozygous recessive, an alternative phenotype results.
Duplicate dominant epistasis (15:1): A dominant allele at either of two loci is sufficient to produce the same phenotype.
Duplicate genes with cumulative effect (9:6:1) and dominant and recessive interaction (13:3) are further recognized variants.

blocks.x: These ratios all still sum to sixteenths, reflecting their origin in an underlying dihybrid (AaBb × AaBb) cross whose 9:3:3:1 classes have simply been regrouped by phenotype. A worked sweet-pea style example: gene C is required for any color (cc = white regardless of other genotype), while gene R/r determines red vs. blue when color is expressed. A cross Cc Rr × Cc Rr gives 9 C_R_ (red) : 3 C_rr (blue-ish, depending on dominance direction) : ... which can appear experimentally as ratios like 3/8 red : 3/8 blue (or similar) : 1/4 white, reflecting the epistatic masking of R/r phenotype whenever cc is present.

Complementation is a related but distinct concept: when two different recessive mutant alleles (in different genes) are combined in a hybrid and the wild-type phenotype is restored, the mutations are said to complement one another, indicating they lie in different genes (as opposed to codominance, which describes simultaneous expression of two alleles at one gene).

Some alleles, when present in a particular dosage (often homozygous), cause death of the organism before or shortly after birth, distorting the expected Mendelian ratios. A classic example is coat color in mice: the yellow allele (AY) is dominant for coat color but homozygous lethal (AYAY embryos die), so a cross of two yellow heterozygotes (AYa × AYa) yields surviving offspring in a 2:1 ratio (yellow:agouti) rather than the naive 3:1, because the homozygous dominant class is removed from the pool of survivors.

Many traits — height, skin color, IQ-type measures, crop yield — are controlled not by a single gene but by the additive, small effects of many genes acting together, often further modified by environmental influence. Because multiple loci each contribute incrementally, polygenic traits typically show continuous variation along a bell-shaped (normal) distribution in a population, rather than falling into a small number of sharply discrete phenotypic classes. This means the statement that "polygenic traits are expressed as absolute or discrete characters" is considered true only in the specific, narrow sense used by some exam sources to describe threshold traits, but conventionally and more accurately, polygenic/quantitative traits are recognized precisely for producing continuous, graded variation rather than the sharp either/or categories typical of single-gene Mendelian traits — be prepared for either framing depending on how your instructor phrases it, but understand the underlying biology: many genes, small additive effects, environmental modulation, continuous distribution.

items: Penetrance is the proportion of individuals with a given genotype who actually show the expected phenotype at all (all-or-none, population-level measure). Incomplete penetrance means some individuals carrying the genotype show no phenotype whatsoever.

Expressivity describes the degree or severity to which the phenotype is expressed in those individuals who do show it (a within-individual, graded measure). Variable expressivity is the term for when a phenotype is expressed to differing degrees among individuals sharing the same genotype.

Huntington disease is a well-known example of an autosomal dominant trait with locus on chromosome 4p (4pter region) that shows complete but age-dependent penetrance — virtually everyone who inherits the mutant allele eventually develops the disease, but onset is typically delayed until mid-adulthood.

Some female carriers of X-linked recessive conditions (e.g., hemophilia B) can show mild symptoms despite being heterozygous carriers; the most common explanation is skewed X-inactivation, where the X chromosome carrying the normal allele happens to be inactivated (per Lyon's hypothesis / lyonization) in a majority of the woman's cells, effectively unmasking the mutant allele's phenotype in most of her tissue.

sections.title: Autosomal vs. X-Linked Inheritance and Pedigree Analysis

blocks.x: Recognizing an inheritance pattern in a pedigree relies on a handful of diagnostic clues:

items: Autosomal dominant: Affected individuals typically have at least one affected parent (no skipped generations in a fully penetrant trait); affected × unaffected matings produce roughly equal numbers of affected and unaffected offspring; both sexes affected equally. Examples: Marfan syndrome, achondroplasia, Huntington disease.

Autosomal recessive: Affected individuals often arise from two unaffected (carrier) parents; trait can skip generations; both sexes equally affected; consanguinity increases risk. Examples: Tay-Sachs disease, Bloom syndrome, Fanconi anemia, and albinism. Nail-Patella syndrome is actually autosomal dominant, not recessive — a frequently misstated fact on exams.

X-linked recessive: Affects males far more often than females (males are hemizygous for the X); an affected father cannot pass the trait to his sons (no male-to-male transmission); daughters of affected fathers are obligate carriers. Classic historical example: the descendants of Queen Victoria, several of whose male descendants were affected by haemophilia (an X-linked recessive clotting disorder) — not deafness, cancer, or colour-blindness in that specific pedigree, though colour-blindness is itself a separate, common X-linked recessive trait used in other classic pedigree problems. Androgenetic alopecia (male-pattern baldness) is often taught as X-linked recessive-influenced in simplified pedigree exercises.

X-linked dominant: Affects both sexes, but often more severely or more frequently in females; no male-to-male transmission; affected fathers pass the trait to all daughters but no sons. Aicardi syndrome is a notable example of an X-linked dominant condition (often listed as X-linked recessive in flawed quiz keys, but the correct classification is X-linked dominant, and this is typically the "incorrect match" answer on such items).

blocks.x: Autosomal dominant traits, despite being easy to trace in pedigrees, are in practice comparatively uncommon/infrequent in populations relative to recessive traits, since dominant deleterious alleles are exposed to selection in every generation (heterozygotes are affected), whereas recessive deleterious alleles can be hidden and propagated silently in unaffected carriers.

Mendelian genetics is fundamentally probabilistic, and standard rules of probability (the product rule for independent, simultaneous events; the sum rule for mutually exclusive alternative outcomes) apply directly to genetic predictions.

items: For two parents each heterozygous for an autosomal recessive condition (e.g., albinism, Aa × Aa), each child independently has a 3/4 chance of being unaffected and 1/4 chance of being affected. The probability that two children are phenotypically identical to one another (both unaffected or both affected) is (3/4)² + (1/4)² = 9/16 + 1/16 = 10/16 = 5/8.

Combined multi-gene probability problems require multiplying independent probabilities across each gene. For example, if a father has a rare autosomal dominant condition (achondroplasia) and is otherwise unrelated in genotype to a maternal X-linked recessive colour-blindness carrier situation, the joint probability of a specific combined outcome (e.g., child is colourblind and of normal height) is found by multiplying the individual-trait probabilities together (in a representative worked problem of this type, the answer comes to 1/8).

For crosses tracking several independently assorting genes across two parents with different genotypes at each locus, the proportion of offspring matching a specified target phenotype is calculated by multiplying together the independent probability for each gene separately (e.g., a five-gene cross of the form Aa Bb cc Dd ee × Aa bb Cc Dd asking for the proportion identical to one specific parent works out, gene-by-gene, to a combined fraction such as 9/64).

sections.title: Linkage: The Exception to Independent Assortment

blocks.x: Genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together rather than assorting independently, because physical proximity reduces the frequency of recombination (crossing over) between them. Linked genes do not obey the law of independent assortment — this is precisely why linkage is considered an important exception to one of Mendel's two laws. Genetic recombination in the classical Mendelian sense (production of novel allele combinations not seen in the parents) arises through independent assortment of unlinked genes (and, at finer scale, through crossing over between linked genes); linkage itself, mutation, and incomplete dominance are not sources of this recombination in the same direct sense. A Punnett square remains the standard tool for predicting and visualizing the probable genotypic and phenotypic outcomes of any cross, linked or unlinked.

Human and experimental genetics rely on several complementary analytical tools: pedigree analysis (tracing trait transmission through families), karyotyping (visualizing chromosome number/structure), and RFLP (restriction fragment length polymorphism) analysis (a molecular marker technique for linkage/mapping studies). A classic test cross, by contrast, is a tool primarily suited to experimental organisms with controlled matings and is not typically usable for analyzing human pedigrees, since researchers cannot arrange human matings experimentally.
